PrimeMart Retail Inc. - Q3 FY2024 Earnings Call Transcript

Operator:
Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the PrimeMart Retail Inc. Q3 FY2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. [Operator Instructions] Please also note, today's event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Johnson, Vice President of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Johnson, Vice President of Investor Relations:
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, and thank you for joining us today to discuss PrimeMart Retail's results for the Q3 FY2024. Joining me on today’s call are Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer; Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer; and David Ramirez, Chief Merchandising Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that this call contains forward-looking statements, which are subject to risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

With that, I’ll turn the call over to Mike Thompson.

Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Thank you, Sarah. Good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. I’m pleased to report PrimeMart Retail's performance for the Q3 FY2024. We continued to execute on our strategic priorities and delivered solid results despite the challenging macroeconomic environment.

Today I will cover five key aspects of our performance. First, our overall performance showed resilience with comparable store sales up 3.1% amid moderating consumer demand, supported by our stores-first omnichannel approach. Second, e-commerce growth accelerated through buy-online-pick-up-in-store and ship-from-store, contributing meaningfully to traffic and sales uplift. Third, store performance remained strong, with productivity gains driving margin expansion. Fourth, our marketing initiatives, particularly digital efforts, boosted foot traffic and return on ad spend. And fifth, supply chain optimization, including inventory discipline, helped us navigate disruptions effectively.

We are confident in our ability to navigate the current environment and deliver long-term value for our shareholders.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Lisa Chen to provide more details on our financial results.

Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer:
Thank you, Mike. Good morning. I'll provide a more detailed review of our financial performance for the Q3 FY2024. Our total revenue for the quarter was $18.4 billion, a 3.5% increase compared to the same period last year, driven by a mix of new store contributions and solid comps. Gross margin expanded to 38.5%, primarily driven by private label penetration, reduced markdowns, and supply chain efficiencies that shaved freight costs. Operating expenses were $4.2 billion, representing 22.7% of revenue, reflecting leverage in labor and targeted marketing spend. Net income came in at $850 million, or $1.52 per share. We generated $1.3 billion in cash flow from operations, underscoring our strong free cash flow conversion. Inventory levels are currently well-controlled, positioning us for the holiday ramp.

As we dive deeper, let's start with inventory management, which remains a cornerstone of our brick-and-mortar operational efficiency. Inventory has been pivotal amid moderating consumer demand, ongoing supply chain headwinds from Red Sea disruptions, and our shift toward omnichannel where stores act as micro-distribution hubs. Ending inventory stood at $1.28 billion as of quarter-end, a 4.2% increase year-over-year from $1.23 billion in Q3 FY2023. On a comparable store basis, that's a 2.8% YoY rise, adjusted for our 15 new store openings in high-density suburban markets. This puts us ahead of peers—our inventory-to-sales ratio improved to 28.4% from 30.1% last year, even with a 3.1% comp sales decline. Inventory turns sped up to 5.2x for the quarter, up from 4.8x YoY, fueling that 120 basis point gross margin expansion through fewer markdowns.

By category in our diversified model across apparel, home essentials, and consumer durables: Apparel and softlines, 52% of inventory, rose 6.1% YoY to $665 million, as we pre-positioned for holidays with extra cold-weather outerwear and athleisure from vendors like Patagonia-inspired lines and our private-label ActiveEdge brand. Demand forecasting accuracy jumped 18% thanks to our AI tool, EchoForecast, cutting stockouts by 22% in key SKUs, though fashion-forward denim turns softened 10% YoY as consumers traded down amid inflation, much like at Gap Inc. Home goods and hardlines, 28% of inventory, held flat YoY at $358 million, normalizing after the 2022 home refresh boom—bedding and small kitchen electrics steady, but we cut big-ticket area rugs by 8% via vendor-managed inventory programs similar to Home Depot's, dodging the overstock issues Macy's faced last holiday. Consumer electronics and seasonal, 20% of inventory, dropped 5.3% YoY to $257 million, emphasizing just-in-time for high-velocity items like wireless earbuds and smart home devices, à la Best Buy, while trimming Halloween and early holiday merch by 12% to match cautious back-to-school comps.

Regionally, across our 1,250 locations in 45 states: Northeast and Midwest, 45% of inventory, up 7.2% YoY on strong urban foot traffic in flagships like Chicago and Boston, with cold-weather builds and days inventory outstanding at 52 days versus 58 last year. Southeast, 30% of inventory, up 3.4% YoY, aided by hurricane recovery restocking in Florida and Georgia, where our store-as-hub model boosted BOPIS shipments 25%. West Coast, 25% of inventory, down 2.1% YoY due to caution on softer California comps and port delays—we shifted 15% of stock to Reno cross-docking, trimming lead times by 4 days.

Enabling this were RFID tagging now in 85% of stores, up from 60%, improving shrink reduction by 14% and feeding real-time data into our SAP demand planning. Our Blue Yonder partnership rationalized 1,200 SKUs, cutting slow-movers by $45 million, while dual-sourcing from Vietnam and Mexico stabilized COGS against China tariffs. We're prioritizing high-turn, high-margin hero SKUs, using flash sales and our app for aged inventory liquidation—92% under 120 days old, up from 87% YoY. For Q4 and FY2025, we see 2-4% YoY inventory growth with turns at 5.0x+, supporting our 8-10% EBITDA growth target.

Shifting to labor costs and store payroll leverage, another area of operational excellence. In brick-and-mortar retail, labor is our largest controllable SG&A item, typically 10-12% of sales. Store labor costs hit 10.6% of net sales, down 90 basis points YoY from 11.5%, saving $28 million on a comp basis despite 5.2% comp growth—our best since pre-pandemic. Total store payroll rose just 0.8% YoY, 40 basis points below sales growth, expanding store-level margins by 110 basis points to 8.4%, outperforming Target's deleverage and matching Home Depot's gains.

Traffic up 3.1% comp from private label and back-to-school let us keep hours flat at 14.2 million across 1,850 stores. Sales per labor hour climbed 4.8% to $142, with productivity index at a record 108. Our UKG Pro platform with Revelry Labs AI hit 92% scheduling accuracy using weather, competitor foot traffic from Placer.ai, and inventory data—reducing overstaffing 12% in non-peaks while maintaining 95% on-shelf availability. The Associate Hub app has 65% adoption, enabling self-scheduling and cross-training for 25% more omnichannel fulfillment, as self-checkout hit 42% of transactions with NCR computer vision keeping shrink under 1.1%.

Regionally, Sunbelt markets (32% of stores) leveraged 120 basis points at $16.20 average hourly, thanks to clustering. Coastal high-cost areas like California and Northeast (28%) saw 60 basis points leverage amid wage hikes to $16.50, offset by incentives tied to NPS—$14 million in variable pay. Tenure up 18% to 2.8 years, attrition down to 22% via MartU upskilling for 12,000 associates. For Q3, we expect 50-75 basis points leverage on 3-4% comps and 4.1% wage growth, with holiday hours up just 2% versus 5% sales lift.

On digital marketing effectiveness, a key growth lever for our 1,200 stores generating 78% of $4.2 billion TTM revenue in home goods and beyond. We spent $45 million digitally, up 22% YoY but down to 8.5% of SG&A from 10.2%, delivering 6.8x blended ROAS—28% better than Q3 2022's 5.3x, topping Target's 5.1x and Macy's 4.9x. Google Ads at 8.2x on $18 million via dynamic remarketing for 'sectional sofas near me'; Meta at 5.4x on $12 million with 15% store conversion lift from loyalty app pixels.

Using GA4 and MMM with first-party data from 28 million rewards members, we cut attribution leakage 35%. Geofencing within 10 miles drove 1.2 million store visits, per Google, lifting ATV 18% to $145 via upsell bundles. Sun Belt (420 stores) saw 7.5x ROAS and 22% traffic growth on patio trends; Northeast at 5.9x countered by DOOH pilots yielding 3.2x and 9% lift. U.K. stores at 6.1x via Criteo. Post-cookie, 62% budget contextual/probabilistic; Tealium CDP integrates POS/app/WiFi for personalization—Store Dayparting boosted midday traffic 27%, CPA to $12.50. Shoppable Reels with AR at 4.2% CTR drive 32% BOPIS.

Our HomeStyle Ad Network in 800 stores generates $15 million at 12x ROAS. Pilots on Roku CTV show 7.1x and 2.5x LTV. This accelerates $300 million annual traffic, underpinning 65% of comp growth.

Regional performance variations further highlight our agility. Comps up 4.2% overall on 2.1% traffic and 2.0% basket, margins +110 bps to 38.4%. Northeast (28% sales, 340 stores): +6.8% comps, +4.3% traffic on remodels/patio (+12%), AUR +3.2%, but shrink at 1.8%—RFID and TyTech AI to cut 30%. Midwest (25%, 310 stores): +3.9%, UPT +1.7% on tools/HVAC, Peak Pro program +15% contractor sales, 12 Efficiency Hub remodels. South (30%, 370 stores): +7.2%, housing boom +9%, hardlines +18%, traffic +5.2%, Atlanta DC cuts BOPIS times 25%, $150 million for 25 new stores. West Coast (15%, 180 stores): -0.5%, traffic -2.1% on layoffs, but sustainable lines +22%; closing 8, converting 15 to experiential, Zipline drones -40% out-of-stocks. Canada +2.1%.

These variations reflect our regional agility via Manhattan Associates OMS at ZIP-level 92% accuracy, stabilizing e-comm cannibalization at 18%.

Finally, our outlook for Q4 FY2024 and full FY2025. Q2 EPS beat at $1.52 on 4.2% comps and +120 bps margins. For Q4, net sales $18.3-$18.6 billion, 3-4% comps; ex-grocery 2.5-3.5%; gross margin 28.2-28.5% on private label to 32%, RFID shrink cuts, Memphis DC +18% throughput. SG&A 22.8-23.1% with $75 million savings; EPS $1.68-$1.76; FCF $1.2-$1.4 billion. Southeast/Sunbelt +5%+ comps; Northeast/Midwest flat to +1%; Canada 2%.

Full-year: sales $72.5-$73.5 billion, 3.5-4.5% growth, 3.8-4.8% comps; gross 28.1-28.4% on omnichannel (BOPIS/ship-from-store 25%), $200 million rebates; SG&A 23.0-23.3% with $300 million tech savings, turns to 7.2x; op income $4.85-$5.05 billion, EPS $6.45-$6.75 (+8%), debt/EBITDA 2.1x, capex $4.2 billion (EV charging, clinics). Pillars: value leadership, tech stores (AR +15% conversion), adjacencies ($500 million health sales FY2026). Risks: tariffs, unemployment >4.2%, buffered by $8 billion liquidity.

We are maintaining a strong balance sheet and are well positioned to invest in our growth initiatives.

Now, I'd like to hand it over to David Ramirez, our Chief Merchandising Officer, to discuss our new product lines.

David Ramirez, Chief Merchandising Officer:
Thank you, Lisa. This quarter, we launched our ActiveEdge apparel line, which has seen strong initial uptake with 22% reduction in stockouts and double-digit sales growth in athleisure categories, driving higher margins through private-label innovation. We're excited about the potential of this new product and other upcoming launches like expanded sustainable home essentials.

Now, let's open the line for questions.

Operator:
Thank you. [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from John Smith with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

John Smith (Goldman Sachs):
Good morning. Can you provide more color on the impact of inflation on your sales?

Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Good morning, John. Inflation continues to pressure discretionary categories like apparel and electronics, where we've seen consumers trading down, similar to industry trends. However, our value positioning with private labels at 32% mix and dynamic pricing has offset this, delivering 3-4% comps. Essentials remain resilient, and we're capturing share through targeted promotions.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Emily Davis with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Emily Davis (JPMorgan):
What are your expectations for same-store sales growth in the next quarter?

Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer:
Thanks, Emily. For Q4, we're guiding 3-4% comps, with strength in Sunbelt regions at 5%+ from housing and curbside growth, offset by modest Northeast traffic. This assumes continued value-seeking, supported by AI pricing across 70% of stores and holiday BOPIS surges.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Robert Lee with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Robert Lee (Barclays):
Can you elaborate on the supply chain improvements?

Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Absolutely, Robert. Our Memphis DC automation boosted throughput 18%, cross-docking in Reno cut West Coast lead times 4 days, and dual-sourcing mitigated tariffs. RFID at 85% of stores and Blue Yonder optimization trimmed $45 million in slow inventory, turning 5.2x and protecting margins.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Anna Patel with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Anna Patel (Morgan Stanley):
How are labor productivity trends holding up regionally?

Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer:
Great question, Anna. Sunbelt leveraged 120 bps on lower wages and clustering, while coasts managed 60 bps via incentives despite hikes. Overall SPLH up 4.8% to $142, with AI scheduling at 92% accuracy driving the leverage.

Operator:
Thank you. That concludes today's questions.

Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Thank you for your questions. In closing, we are pleased with our progress this quarter and remain focused on executing our long-term strategy. Thank you for your continued support.

Sarah Johnson, Vice President of Investor Relations:
This concludes today's call. Thank you for joining us.
